phases.name: Paperwork
phases.when: Day one, in parallel with everything
phases.goal: Start the clocks you do not control.
work: Production app registration with Epic, Oracle Health and athenahealth
NLM UMLS licence (covers SNOMED CT in the US); AMA licence for CPT/HCPCS
BAAs with every subprocessor that touches PHI — hosting, model API, voice if used
HIPAA control baseline and the evidence-collection tooling behind it
phases.exit: Nothing. This phase never exits — it only has to have started.
phases.note: Everything on the build sheet is buildable and none of it is the expensive part. The expensive part is registration: it takes weeks to months per vendor, runs on someone else's calendar, and no code shortens it.

phases.name: One source, end to end
phases.goal: A real Bundle from a real server, in your own Postgres.
work: Source catalog seeded with one sandbox — Epic's is the obvious choice
SMART backend services launch, one token stored encrypted
Pull Patient, Condition and Observation. Nothing else
raw_resources table with the idempotent unique key
phases.exit: You can point at a row and say where it came from and when.
phases.note: Resist breadth here. A second source before the state machine exists buys nothing and costs a refactor.

phases.name: Make it survive
phases.goal: Turn the demo into a system.
work: Connection state machine, transactional outbox, append-only auth_events
Proactive token refresh at T-10 minutes, rotated tokens persisted in-transaction
Pagination to the end of link[next]; per-source rate limiting; backoff honouring Retry-After
pull_runs monitoring table and the first OpenTelemetry traces
phases.exit: A pull survives a token rotation and a 429 storm without human intervention.
phases.note: This phase is invisible in a demo and is the whole difference between a prototype and a product.

phases.name: Make it usable
phases.goal: A second engineer can onboard a source without you.
work: Workspaces with row-level security on every table
Environment-prefixed API keys, hashed at rest
The read API with keyset pagination, and two signed webhooks
The operations dashboard — connection states, pull history, export runs
phases.exit: Support can answer "is it broken or is it empty?" without a database client.
phases.note: Put workspace_id on every table from the first one. Retrofitting it is the most tedious migration you will ever run.

phases.name: Make it plural
work: Per-vendor quirk table for scope strings and discovery deviations
Resource lists driven by CapabilityStatement rather than constants
Bulk $export for the backend pattern
Whatever the registrations from P0 have actually cleared
phases.exit: Adding a source is configuration and waiting, not new code.
phases.note: Mostly calendar, not engineering. If P0 was not started on day one, this is where the schedule slips.

phases.name: Make it mean something
phases.goal: Data you can ask clinical questions of.
work: Terminology: LOINC and RxNorm loaded; SNOMED server standing up
Derived clinical domain models with provenance back to raw
Negative-finding queries — "this does not exist anywhere" as a first-class answer
Deterministic patient matching, with a human review queue behind the probabilistic tier
phases.exit: "Six weeks of documented conservative therapy" answers as a query, not a search.
phases.note: Deliberately last of the platform phases. Normalise once you have real variety to normalise against, not before.

phases.name: Pre-auth vertical slice
phases.goal: One payer, one service line, a human gate, a real approval.
work: CRD check at order-select, inside the five-second hook budget
Policy pack: the top five policies of one payer, curated by hand
Form engine and CQL prefill; unanswerable items left visibly blank
Packet assembly, the coordinator review screen, and the approval gate
Tier-1 payer only — PAS submit and Subscription decision push
phases.exit: A named coordinator approves a packet and a payer returns an authorisation number.
phases.note: This is the demo in this prototype, made real. Nothing about it requires the second or third payer tier to exist.

phases.name: The other two payer tiers
phases.goal: One workflow, three transports, identical agents.
work: X12 278/275/277 through a clearinghouse, with per-payer enrollment
Supervised portal automation for the tier-3 payers worth serving
EHR write-back of authorisation number, validity window and reference
Document and OCR ingestion for outside records
phases.exit: Switching a payer from tier 3 to tier 1 changes one catalog row and no agent code.
phases.note: If this is not true at the end of the phase, the integration layer leaked into the workflow.

phases.name: Appeals, memory, tenant two
phases.goal: Compounding, and proof it compounds for someone else.
work: Denial classification, appeal packet assembly, clinician signature gate
Agent memory scoped hard to the tenant, with the governance boundary written down
Second tenant onboarded through the dashboard rather than by an engineer
Confidence calibrated against the first tenant's historical determinations
phases.exit: The second tenant's onboarding is measured in days and does not touch a code branch.
phases.note: The first customer is also the first calibration partner. That is contractually messy and worth negotiating before signing, not after.

decisions.why: Resource validation, search parameters and reference resolution are several months you would otherwise reinvent slightly wrong.

decisions.pick: archetype discipline now, CDR when a second workflow needs it
decisions.why: openEHR buys a genuinely longitudinal, archetype-governed record. It also buys a second modelling discipline, a smaller hiring pool and a mapping layer. Take the modelling discipline into the derived layer first; the CDR is a decision you can still make in month nine, and a rewrite you cannot undo in month three.
Never hand-roll SNOMED subsumption. Own the value-set versioning on top of it, not the subsumption itself.
BullMQ gives retries, backoff and concurrency in an afternoon. Move when a single pull spans hours and must survive a deploy mid-crawl.
Several EHR vendors deviate from strict OIDC discovery. Override in a table; never patch the library.
Retries, dead-lettering and signature rotation are a solved commodity and cheaper to rent than to own.

decisions.pick: A clearinghouse — TriZetto, Availity or Optum
decisions.why: There is no version of building an X12 278 stack that ends well. Enrollment per payer still takes days to weeks; price that in.

decisions.pick: build narrowly, or refuse the segment
decisions.why: Brittle, breaks on every payer UI change, and the only route to a large share of payers today. Both answers are defensible; drifting into it is not.
SSO will be asked for in the first enterprise conversation, not the fifth.

decisions.pick: AWS KMS or Vault, one key per environment
decisions.why: Envelope-encrypt every token with a per-workspace data key. One key for the whole platform is a finding waiting for an auditor.

decisions.item: Source catalog, state machine, pull engine, derived models, policy store
decisions.why: These five are the product. Everything else on this list is plumbing you should rent.

risks.note: Weeks to months per EHR vendor, entirely outside your control. The single most common cause of a slipped healthcare integration date.
Payer policies arrive as PDFs and change without notice. Curation is an operations function with a permanent headcount, not a project with an end date.
Hand-authored constants are not calibration. Real numbers need a customer's labelled history, which makes the first customer the first training partner.
Breaks on every payer UI change. Needs change detection, an on-call owner, and a human on every submission.
An EHR's token must never be forwarded outside the boundary that issued it. Cheap to design for, expensive to retrofit.
CPT is AMA-licensed with a real per-seat cost. Discovering it during procurement is worse than budgeting for it now.
A duplicate is a data-quality problem; a false merge is a clinical safety incident. Probabilistic matching needs a human adjudication queue from day one.
Deferring the CDR is recoverable. Adopting it and reversing is not — it propagates into every derived model and every query.

Plans that expose these APIs only because they are compelled to will expose them unevenly. The legacy tier stays load-bearing for years; plan for a 2028 where half the surface is still portal and fax.
The compounding asset and the sharpest governance risk in the product. Enforce it at the storage boundary, not in application code.
